why: One coffee works mainly by blocking adenosine A2A receptors, which only indirectly and weakly changes striatal dopamine release; human PET displacement studies are largely negative.
source: Volkow et al., Transl Psychiatry 2015 (caffeine raises D2/D3 receptor availability, not dopamine release); Ferre, J Neurochem 2008 (adenosine-dopamine receptor interactions)

why: Caffeine is a competitive antagonist at adenosine receptors, so it blocks the signal without lowering (or raising) the amount of adenosine in the tissue.
source: Fredholm et al., Pharmacol Rev 1999; Porkka-Heiskanen & Kalinchuk, Sleep Med Rev 2011

why: Caffeine modestly raises sympathetic outflow and plasma/central noradrenaline, more in people who do not drink it regularly.
source: Robertson et al., NEJM 1978; Lane et al., Psychosom Med 2002

why: A ~100 mg dose produces a clear but moderate rise in cortisol in non-habituated people; regular drinkers show a much blunted response.
source: Lovallo et al., Psychosom Med 2005; Lovallo et al., Pharmacol Biochem Behav 2006

why: An oral 10-20 mg dose blocks roughly half of striatal dopamine transporters and raises extracellular dopamine by a clear but sub-amphetamine amount.
source: Volkow et al., J Neurosci 2001 (oral MPH, [11C]raclopride); Volkow et al., Am J Psychiatry 1998 (DAT occupancy)

why: In prefrontal cortex methylphenidate raises dopamine mostly via noradrenaline-transporter blockade; rodent microdialysis shows a clear rise, scaled down for a therapeutic human dose.
source: Berridge et al., Biol Psychiatry 2006; Hannestad et al., Biol Psychiatry 2010 (human NET occupancy)

why: Methylphenidate is a potent noradrenaline reuptake blocker with high human NET occupancy at clinical doses.
source: Hannestad et al., Biol Psychiatry 2010; Berridge et al., Biol Psychiatry 2006

why: Methylphenidate has very low affinity for the serotonin transporter, so cortical serotonin is essentially unchanged.
source: Han & Gu, BMC Pharmacol 2006 (transporter selectivity); Kuczenski & Segal, J Neurochem 1997

why: Dexamphetamine reverses the dopamine transporter and empties vesicles, producing a larger striatal dopamine rise than methylphenidate; human PET displacement at 0.2-0.3 mg/kg is robust.
source: Drevets et al., Biol Psychiatry 2001 ([11C]raclopride, oral/IV amphetamine); Laruelle et al., Synapse 1995

why: Amphetamine raises prefrontal dopamine clearly, though with a flatter dose-response than striatum; rodent microdialysis scaled to a 10 mg human dose.
source: Kuczenski & Segal, J Neurosci 1995; Narendran et al., Synapse 2014 (human cortical amphetamine challenge)

why: Amphetamine is roughly as potent a noradrenaline releaser as a dopamine releaser.
source: Rothman et al., Synapse 2001 (releasing potencies at DAT/NET/SERT)

why: Dexamphetamine is roughly an order of magnitude weaker at releasing serotonin than catecholamines, so the serotonin rise at a 10 mg dose is small.
source: Rothman et al., Synapse 2001; Kuczenski & Segal, J Neurochem 1997

why: Methamphetamine is a more lipophilic and longer-acting releaser than amphetamine and produces the largest striatal dopamine rise of the common stimulants; rodent values are far higher and are shrunk here for a human recreational dose.
source: Rothman et al., Synapse 2001; Melega et al., Synapse 1995 (primate); Kirkpatrick et al., Psychopharmacology 2012

why: Methamphetamine is a potent noradrenaline releaser, which drives its cardiovascular and arousal effects; rodent values are higher and are shrunk here for a human recreational dose.
source: Rothman et al., Synapse 2001 (releasing potencies at DAT/NET/SERT)

why: Methamphetamine releases serotonin too, but several-fold less potently than dopamine, which is why it is less empathogenic than MDMA.
source: Rothman et al., Synapse 2001; Baumann et al., Neuropsychopharmacology 2011

why: Intranasal cocaine blocks 60-80% of striatal dopamine transporters, giving a large but transporter-limited dopamine rise (it blocks reuptake rather than forcing release).
source: Volkow et al., Nature 1997 (human DAT occupancy); Hurd & Ungerstedt, Synapse 1989

why: Cocaine blocks the noradrenaline transporter with similar affinity to DAT, raising cortical noradrenaline.
source: Ritz et al., Science 1987; Rothman et al., Synapse 2001

why: Unlike amphetamine, cocaine blocks the serotonin transporter about as well as DAT, so cortical serotonin rises clearly.
source: Ritz et al., Science 1987; Bradberry et al., J Neurochem 1993

why: MDMA's defining action is massive carrier-mediated serotonin release; rodent microdialysis shows 10-20x at higher doses, shrunk here for 100 mg in a human.
source: Rothman et al., Synapse 2001; Baumann et al., Neuropsychopharmacology 2008; Green et al., Pharmacol Rev 2003

why: MDMA also releases dopamine, but roughly ten-fold less potently than serotonin, which is why it feels different from amphetamine.
source: Rothman et al., Synapse 2001; Green et al., Pharmacol Rev 2003

why: MDMA is a strong noradrenaline releaser, which accounts for much of the heart-rate, blood-pressure and arousal response.
source: Rothman et al., Synapse 2001; Hysek et al., Clin Pharmacol Ther 2012 (reboxetine blocks MDMA cardiostimulation)

why: MDMA reliably raises plasma oxytocin in controlled human studies, and the rise tracks the feeling of closeness.
source: Dumont et al., Soc Neurosci 2009; Kirkpatrick et al., Psychopharmacology 2014; Hysek et al., SCAN 2014

why: MDMA produces one of the largest drug-induced cortisol rises measured in humans, severalfold above baseline.
source: Mas et al., J Pharmacol Exp Ther 1999; Harris et al., Psychopharmacology 2002; Seibert et al., Psychopharmacology 2014

why: A single 50 mg dose blocks the serotonin transporter, but 5-HT1A autoreceptor feedback damps the rise, so forebrain serotonin goes up only modestly on day one.
source: Meyer et al., Am J Psychiatry 2004 (human SERT occupancy); Bel & Artigas, Eur J Pharmacol 1993; Invernizzi et al., Brain Res 1992

why: Sertraline has some DAT affinity in vitro, but at 50 mg the occupancy is negligible and striatal dopamine is essentially unchanged acutely.
source: Kugaya et al., Am J Psychiatry 2003 (no measurable DAT occupancy at clinical sertraline doses); Owens et al., J Pharmacol Exp Ther 1997

why: After weeks of dosing the 5-HT1A autoreceptor brake desensitises, so the same transporter block now produces a much larger sustained rise than on day one - the usual account of the delayed antidepressant effect.
source: Blier & de Montigny, Trends Pharmacol Sci 1994; Bel & Artigas, Synapse 1993; Rutter et al., J Neurochem 1994

why: Sertraline is selective for the serotonin transporter; chronic treatment does not meaningfully raise cortical noradrenaline.
source: Owens et al., J Pharmacol Exp Ther 1997; Beique et al., Br J Pharmacol 1998

why: Despite its reputation, bupropion occupies only about 20-30% of striatal dopamine transporters at clinical doses, so the dopamine rise is small.
source: Learned-Coughlin et al., Biol Psychiatry 2003 (human DAT occupancy ~26%); Meyer et al., Am J Psychiatry 2002

why: Bupropion and its hydroxy metabolite act mainly as noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors and releasers, the larger of its two monoamine actions.
source: Dong & Blier, Psychopharmacology 2001; Stahl et al., Prim Care Companion J Clin Psychiatry 2004

why: Bupropion has essentially no affinity for the serotonin transporter, which is why it lacks SSRI-type sexual and gastrointestinal side effects.
source: Dong & Blier, Psychopharmacology 2001; Stahl et al., Prim Care Companion J Clin Psychiatry 2004

why: Irreversible non-selective MAO inhibition stops the main breakdown route for serotonin, so extracellular levels rise several-fold once the enzyme pool is inhibited.
source: Finberg, Pharmacol Ther 2014; Celada & Artigas, Naunyn-Schmiedeberg's Arch Pharmacol 1993

why: MAO-A inhibition raises noradrenaline as well as serotonin; the resulting tyramine sensitivity is the basis of the cheese reaction.
source: Finberg, Pharmacol Ther 2014; Blier & de Montigny, Trends Pharmacol Sci 1994

why: Phenelzine inhibits MAO-B as well as MAO-A, so striatal dopamine, whose main degrading enzyme is MAO-B, also rises.
source: Finberg, Pharmacol Ther 2014; Youdim et al., Nat Rev Neurosci 2006

why: One cigarette produces only a small striatal dopamine release in human PET studies - smaller than most people expect, and several studies find no significant effect in non-deprived smokers.
source: Brody et al., Arch Gen Psychiatry 2004; Barrett et al., Synapse 2004; Montgomery et al., Neuroimage 2007

why: Nicotine acts on presynaptic nicotinic receptors that facilitate cortical acetylcholine release (it does not simply add acetylcholine itself).
source: Wonnacott, Trends Neurosci 1997; Rowell & Winkler, J Neurochem 1984

why: Nicotine stimulates noradrenaline release centrally and peripherally, contributing to its alerting effect.
source: Fu et al., J Pharmacol Exp Ther 1998; Benowitz, NEJM 2010

why: Two drinks produce only a small and variable striatal dopamine signal in human PET; the rise is much smaller than for stimulants and is larger in family-history-positive drinkers.
source: Boileau et al., Synapse 2003; Urban et al., Biol Psychiatry 2010; Yoder et al., Alcohol Clin Exp Res 2007

why: At two drinks the HPA response is small and inconsistent; a clear cortisol rise needs intoxicating doses, so this is a case where a plausible effect is largely absent.
source: Thayer et al., Alcohol Clin Exp Res 2006; Richardson et al., Psychopharmacology 2008 (dose-dependent HPA activation)

why: Oral morphine at an analgesic dose produces only a small striatal dopamine signal in humans; much of opioid euphoria is mu-receptor mediated rather than a large dopamine surge.
source: Hagelberg et al., Pain 2002; Spagnolo et al., Neuropsychopharmacology 2019; Johnson & North, J Neurosci 1992 (disinhibition mechanism)

why: Rapidly delivered heroin disinhibits VTA dopamine neurons and raises accumbens dopamine clearly, though still less than a comparable stimulant dose.
source: Pontieri et al., PNAS 1995; Johnson & North, J Neurosci 1992

why: Human PET studies of smoked or oral THC find only a small dopamine release, and several are null - notably smaller than for stimulants or even alcohol-plus-expectation.
source: Bossong et al., Neuropsychopharmacology 2009; Stokes et al., Neuroimage 2009; Bloomfield et al., Nature 2016 (review)

why: Sub-anaesthetic ketamine blocks NMDA receptors on inhibitory interneurons, disinhibiting cortical pyramidal cells and producing a glutamate surge - the key step in its rapid antidepressant action.
source: Moghaddam et al., J Neurosci 1997; Stone et al., Mol Psychiatry 2012 (human MRS); Abdallah et al., Neuropsychopharmacology 2018

why: Benzodiazepines are positive allosteric modulators: they make each GABA molecule work better at the receptor, they do not increase how much GABA is released.
source: Sigel & Steinmann, J Biol Chem 2012; Rudolph & Knoflach, Nat Rev Drug Discov 2011

why: At an anxiolytic 5 mg dose diazepam does not produce a measurable striatal dopamine release in humans, unlike classic drugs of abuse.
source: Rademacher et al., Psychopharmacology 2016 (no significant [11C]raclopride displacement); Tan et al., Nature 2010 (mechanism is indirect disinhibition)

why: A standard acute psychosocial stressor roughly doubles to quadruples salivary and plasma cortisol, peaking around 20-30 min after the stressor ends.
source: Kirschbaum et al., Neuropsychobiology 1993 (Trier Social Stress Test); Dickerson & Kemeny, Psychol Bull 2004 (meta-analysis)

why: ACTH rises before and proportionally more than cortisol, since it is the pituitary signal that drives the adrenal response.
source: Kirschbaum et al., Neuropsychobiology 1993; Dickerson & Kemeny, Psychol Bull 2004

why: Cortisol rises with exercise above roughly 60% VO2max; an hour of moderate-vigorous exercise gives a clear rise, while light exercise can leave it unchanged.
source: Hill et al., J Endocrinol Invest 2008 (intensity threshold); Luger et al., NEJM 1987

why: Exercise drives the HPA axis from the top, raising ACTH ahead of cortisol.
source: Luger et al., NEJM 1987; Hill et al., J Endocrinol Invest 2008

why: Plasma beta-endorphin rises several-fold after sustained vigorous exercise, and PET shows central opioid release after running.
source: Goldfarb & Jamurtas, Sports Med 1997; Boecker et al., Cereb Cortex 2008 ([11C]diprenorphine after running)

why: Circulating anandamide rises reliably with moderate-intensity exercise and is a better-supported mediator of 'runner's high' than endorphins, which cross the blood-brain barrier poorly.
source: Sparling et al., Neuroreport 2003; Raichlen et al., J Exp Biol 2012; Siebers et al., Psychoneuroendocrinology 2021

why: Sustained noxious stimulation triggers endogenous opioid release, measurable as mu-receptor occupancy changes during experimental pain.
source: Zubieta et al., Science 2001; Bandura-Morgan & Roszkowski, Pain 1986

why: Warm social contact and touch raise plasma oxytocin modestly; effect sizes are small and plasma is an imperfect proxy for central release.
source: Grewen et al., Psychosom Med 2005; Uvnas-Moberg et al., Front Psychol 2014; Leng & Ludwig, Biol Psychiatry 2016 (caveats)

why: CBD inhibits FAAH and anandamide transport, and serum anandamide rose roughly two-fold in a clinical trial - though that trial used far higher doses than 25 mg.
source: Leweke et al., Transl Psychiatry 2012; Bisogno et al., Br J Pharmacol 2001

why: A 0.5-1 mg oral dose pushes blood melatonin far above the natural nocturnal peak, because physiological levels are only tens of picograms per millilitre.
source: Dollins et al., PNAS 1994; Zhdanova et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2001; Vural et al., Drugs Aging 2014

why: Melatonin at sleep-promoting doses is a timing signal, not a stress hormone, and does not meaningfully change evening cortisol.
source: Cagnacci et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 1995; Arendt & Skene, Sleep Med Rev 2005

why: Extended wakefulness accumulates basal-forebrain adenosine, the main biochemical marker of sleep pressure; human A1-receptor PET supports an increase after one night of restriction.
source: Porkka-Heiskanen et al., Science 1997; Elmenhorst et al., J Neurosci 2007 (human A1 receptor upregulation after sleep deprivation)

why: Sleep restriction raises cortisol in the evening, when it should be at its lowest, more than it raises the morning peak - the direction a simulation can easily get wrong.
source: Leproult et al., Sleep 1997; Spiegel et al., Lancet 1999

why: Ghrelin is the pre-meal hunger hormone: it peaks just before eating and is suppressed by about half within an hour of a meal, in proportion to calories.
source: Cummings et al., Diabetes 2001; Callahan et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2004

why: By several hours after a meal ghrelin has climbed back to, and begun to exceed, its pre-meal level as the next hunger episode builds.
source: Cummings et al., Diabetes 2001; Cummings et al., J Clin Invest 2001

why: GLP-1 is secreted by intestinal L-cells in response to nutrients, rising severalfold within 30-60 min of eating.
source: Holst, Physiol Rev 2007; Vilsboll et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2003
